title: The doorpost
hookLine: touching the mezuzah on the way out
tomorrow: the broken tablets went into the Ark. why keep broken pieces?

cards: The third squad of soldiers has one order: don't talk to him. Not a word.

The emperor sent two squads before this one to bring in Onkelos, a Roman who became a Jew, and both times Onkelos talked with them until they became Jews too. So this squad leads him out of his house in silence.
At the door, Onkelos stops and puts his hand on a small case fixed to the doorpost. Then he asks them: what is this? The soldiers have been warned.
But they're curious. You tell us, they say.

teach.h: THE KING IS GUARDED; HERE GOD GUARDS.
teach.b: So he tells them. In this world, a king sits inside, and his servants stand outside to guard him. With the Holy One it's the other way around: His servants sit inside, and He guards them from outside.
Then he quotes a Psalm: the LORD guards your going out and your coming in. The soldiers, the Talmud says, became Jews too, and the emperor sent no more. So what was under his hand?

Deuteronomy says it plainly: "And thou shalt write them upon the door-posts of thy house, and upon thy gates." Write what? The words just before, the Shema: hear, O Israel, and love the LORD with all your heart.
The Hebrew for doorposts is mezuzot, so the little case carries the doorpost's own name: mezuzah. Inside is a scribe's parchment with those paragraphs. And notice where it hangs.
Not on the desk where you study, not by the bed. On the threshold, where you leave.
The words are posted at the exit so they go out with you: into the street, the job, the argument.
Some people touch it on every pass and kiss their fingers. Onkelos touched it on his way to being arrested. Something to tell a friend tonight: the mezuzah is named after the doorpost itself.

how: Jewish homes fix a mezuzah, a case holding a handwritten parchment of the Shema's paragraphs, on the right-hand doorpost of the entrance and often on inner doors; many people touch it, and some kiss their fingers, as they pass.

o: a lucky charm hung above the front entrance
the frame where the mezuzah and its words hang
a short blessing said when leaving the house

games.q: the story and the door — tap the pairs.
p: a Roman who became a Jew
doorpost; the case holding the Shema

s: a mezuzah is a good-luck charm for the house
it holds the words of the Shema, written on the doorposts as Deuteronomy says; the words are the point.
the Hebrew word mezuzah means doorpost
Deuteronomy: write them on the mezuzot, the doorposts of your house.
the mezuzah is meant for the room where you pray
it hangs on the threshold, so the words go out with you.

games.q: you're Onkelos, under arrest, walking out past your own door. the soldiers have orders not to talk. what do you do?
o: go quietly; there's nothing to say to men under orders.
touch the mezuzah and ask them what it is.
argue with them about the emperor's decree.
games.why: he puts his hand on the mezuzah and asks, what is this? his answer, that God guards His people from outside, wins over the third squad too.

practice: Stand up and walk slowly to the nearest doorway. Rest your fingertips on the frame for a moment, the way people touch a mezuzah on the way out, and feel the wood or the paint.
Then step through, unhurried, as though you're carrying something with you.

wordCard.voice: The doorpost: where the mezuzah hangs, holding the Shema's words, touched on the way in and the way out.

orig.note: Hebrew: doorpost; the word in Deuteronomy 6:9, and now the name of the case.

carryVoice: Here's the line: carry the words out. The doorpost is where they leave the house with you.
